title: Fake account suspension / verify-now emails
summary: Messages claiming an account will be suspended, locked, or closed unless the recipient clicks a link and 'verifies' their identity immediately. Legitimate providers rarely threaten immediate suspension over email and never require credential entry through an emailed link.
source: Consumer fraud awareness guidance (industry-standard phishing patterns)

title: OTP / one-time-passcode sharing requests
summary: Scammers impersonate banks or delivery services and ask victims to read out or forward a one-time passcode (OTP) they just received, in order to hijack an account or authorize a fraudulent transaction. No legitimate bank, payment provider, or service will ever ask a customer to share an OTP over phone, SMS, or chat.
indicators: claims to be bank security team

title: Fake lottery, prize, or gift-card winnings
summary: Messages claiming the recipient has won a prize, lottery, or gift card they never entered, requiring a small 'processing fee' or personal details to claim it. This is a classic advance-fee fraud pattern.

title: Unexpected refund or overpayment scams
summary: A message states the recipient is owed a refund or was overpaid, and directs them to a link or asks for banking details to 'process' the refund. These schemes are used to harvest banking credentials or induce fraudulent transfers.

title: Guaranteed-return investment and crypto schemes
summary: Offers promising unusually high, guaranteed, or risk-free returns, often pushing victims to act quickly and to reinvest 'profits.' Legitimate investments always carry risk and disclosure; guarantees of high returns with no risk are a hallmark of Ponzi-style fraud.

title: Cryptocurrency giveaway and wallet-drain scams
summary: Fake celebrity or exchange-branded giveaways asking users to 'send crypto to receive double back,' or fraudulent wallet-connection links designed to drain a victim's crypto wallet.

title: Impersonation of banks, government agencies, or executives
summary: A sender poses as a bank, tax authority, law enforcement agency, or a company executive (CEO fraud / business email compromise) to pressure the recipient into an urgent payment, credential disclosure, or data transfer.

title: Shortened, misspelled, or lookalike domains
summary: Links using URL shorteners, misspelled brand names (typosquatting), unusual top-level domains, or subdomains designed to look like a trusted brand are commonly used to redirect victims to credential-harvesting pages.
indicators: mismatched display text vs actual link
HTTP instead of HTTPS on a login page

title: Urgency and fear-based pressure tactics
summary: Scammers manufacture time pressure ('act within 30 minutes') or fear ('your account has been compromised') to short-circuit careful thinking and push victims toward hasty, unverified action.

title: Fake tech-support and customer-service scams
summary: Unsolicited messages or pop-ups claiming a device is infected or an order has an issue, directing the victim to call a number or install remote-access software, which is then used to steal data or money.
indicators: asks to call a provided number instead of official support

title: Direct requests for passwords or PINs
summary: Any message directly requesting a full password, PIN, or complete card number is a major red flag. Legitimate organizations never ask customers to disclose full passwords or PINs via email, SMS, or chat.
indicators: asks to confirm login details via link

title: Fake delivery / customs fee notifications
summary: Messages impersonating postal or courier services claim a package is held pending a small fee or 'address confirmation,' leading to a phishing page or a card-skimming payment form.
indicators: sender not the actual courier used
